common_name: Cornell Bush Delicata Squash (Compact Non-Vining Delicata)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost into warm, fertile soil in full sun; the compact bush habit fits in far less space than standard vining delicata types, making it a good choice for smaller gardens.

directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing hills to allow the compact bush to fill in without crowding. Cornell Bush Delicata was bred at Cornell University to bring the sweet, nutty, edible-skinned delicata squash into a compact, non-vining bush habit that takes up a fraction of the space of standard vining delicata varieties, making winter squash growing practical in small gardens and raised beds. The oblong, cream-colored fruit striped with green matures with the same rich, sweet, dense orange flesh delicata is prized for, excellent roasted with the thin skin left on. Harvest once the rind has hardened and stripes have deepened in color, and cure fruit in a warm, dry spot for one to two weeks before storing to improve keeping quality.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

common_name: Black Jack Zucchini (Classic High-Yielding Dark Green Zucchini)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; in zone 9, spring-sow February–March and again in late summer for a fall crop.

directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Black Jack is a classic open-pollinated dark green zucchini grown for its vigorous, upright bush habit and dependable, heavy yields of glossy, cylindrical, deep green fruit with tender, mild-flavored flesh. It has long served as a dependable garden standard for gardeners wanting a straightforward, reliable zucchini without the complexity of some newer hybrid disease-resistance packages, performing well across a wide range of soils and conditions. Pick fruit at six to eight inches long for the best flavor and texture, and harvest every day or two once the plant starts producing, since zucchini left on the vine even briefly can balloon rapidly into oversized, seedy, less flavorful fruit.

Starship is a distinctive pale, cream-white zucchini that stands out visually from the far more common dark green types, with smooth, cylindrical fruit and tender, mild flesh good for all standard zucchini preparations, from grilling to sautéing to baking into bread. Beyond its novelty color, the compact, productive bush is a reliable, disease-tolerant performer well suited to home gardens wanting to diversify a summer squash planting beyond the usual green varieties. Pick fruit at six to eight inches for the best eating quality, and harvest frequently once production ramps up, since oversized fruit turns seedy and tough quickly, a trait shared by all zucchini types regardless of skin color.

Safari is a modern hybrid zucchini bred for a strong disease-resistance package, including tolerance to several common squash viruses and powdery mildew, which helps the compact, open bush stay productive and healthy later into the season than many older open-pollinated varieties manage in humid climates. The smooth, dark green, cylindrical fruit has tender, mild flesh typical of good zucchini, and the plant's heavy, sustained yield makes it a solid choice for gardeners who have struggled with squash bugs, vine borers, or mildew shortening the productive life of past plantings. Pick at six to eight inches long for the best texture, and harvest every day or two once fruit begins setting to keep the vigorous plant in steady production.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

common_name: Papaya Pear Squash (Small Pear-Shaped Ornamental-Edible Gourd)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a trellis if space is limited, since vines can sprawl widely.

directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving the sprawling vine plenty of room or a sturdy trellis to climb. Papaya Pear is a small, distinctively pear-shaped squash with pale, mottled skin, harvested young at three to four inches as a tender, mild summer squash for cooking, or left to mature into a firmer, longer-keeping fruit valued as a novelty ornamental for fall displays alongside gourds and pumpkins. This dual-purpose flexibility — usable young in the kitchen or later as an attractive harvest decoration — makes it a fun addition to a vegetable garden looking for something beyond standard zucchini and yellow squash. Pick young fruit every few days for the best culinary texture, or leave select fruit to fully mature and harden for fall display and longer storage.
